cards.prompt: Import seaborn under the alias everyone uses.
cards.why: sns is the universal alias — every tutorial, answer and code review assumes it, so matching the convention makes your code instantly readable to others.
cards.whenToUse: The first line of any seaborn work.
cards.commonMistake: Importing as sb or seaborn, which works but reads as unfamiliar to anyone else.

cards.prompt: Chart average revenue per region with seaborn, without the error bars.
cards.why: This is the seaborn surprise: barplot aggregates for you, and its default is the mean — not the sum. It also draws a 95% confidence interval on every bar unless you pass errorbar=None.
cards.whenToUse: Comparing a typical value across categories, when you want seaborn to do the grouping.
cards.commonMistake: Reading the bars as totals. barplot means 'mean' by default, and the little line on each bar is a confidence interval, not a data range.

cards.prompt: Chart total revenue per region with seaborn.
cards.why: estimator= swaps the aggregation seaborn applies inside each category, so one keyword turns a chart of averages into a chart of totals.
cards.whenToUse: Total volume per category, straight from the raw rows — no groupby needed.
cards.commonMistake: Grouping with pandas first and then also letting seaborn aggregate, which averages values that were already summed.

cards.prompt: Chart how many rows there are per region.
cards.why: countplot is barplot with the aggregation fixed to 'count how many rows', so it takes no y at all — the height *is* the row count.
cards.whenToUse: Showing how a categorical column is distributed.
cards.commonMistake: Passing y='revenue' to countplot and expecting a total; countplot counts rows and ignores the idea of a measured value.

cards.prompt: Count rows per category. Name the keyword that takes the whole DataFrame.
cards.why: Seaborn's core idea: hand it the whole frame once as data=, then refer to columns by *name* as strings. That is why x='category' works where pandas would need df['category'].
cards.whenToUse: Every seaborn call — it is the shape of the entire library.
cards.commonMistake: Passing the Series itself (x=df['category']) out of pandas habit. It works, but you lose the automatic axis labels and the ability to name other columns for hue.

cards.prompt: Total revenue per region, split into a bar per category.
cards.answer: sns.barplot(data=df, x='region', y='revenue', hue='category', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
cards.why: hue= is seaborn's whole answer to a second dimension: name another column and it splits every category into one coloured bar per value, with a legend built for you.
cards.whenToUse: Comparing a metric across two categorical dimensions at once.
cards.commonMistake: Pivoting the frame by hand first. With hue= the long, raw frame is already the right shape.

cards.prompt: Total revenue per region as horizontal bars.
cards.answer: sns.barplot(data=df, x='revenue', y='region', estimator='sum', errorbar=None, orient='h')
cards.why: Seaborn infers orientation from which axis holds the categories, so swapping x and y is usually enough; orient='h' states it outright when the guess would be ambiguous.
cards.whenToUse: Long category names that would collide under vertical bars.
cards.commonMistake: Swapping x and y but leaving the mental model vertical — with horizontal bars the *value* axis is x.

cards.prompt: Show the spread of revenue within each category, not just the average.
cards.why: A bar chart collapses a whole group to one number. A box shows five: the median rule, the box spanning the middle half of the data, and whiskers out to the range.
cards.whenToUse: When 'how spread out is it' matters as much as 'how big is it'.
cards.commonMistake: Reading the box as the full range. The box is the middle 50%; the whiskers carry the rest.

cards.prompt: Show the shape of the revenue distribution in each category, not just its quartiles.
cards.why: A violin is a box plot with the density drawn on: where the shape is wide, values cluster. It reveals two humps where a box plot would show one bland middle.
cards.whenToUse: Checking whether a group is actually one cluster or several.
cards.commonMistake: Trusting the smooth shape on tiny samples. The curve is an estimate, and with a handful of rows it invents detail the data can't support.

cards.prompt: Show revenue for every region-and-category combination as a coloured grid, with the numbers written in.
cards.why: heatmap takes a table that is already the shape of the grid — index becomes the rows, columns become the columns — so the pivot does the work and heatmap only colours it.
cards.whenToUse: Two categorical dimensions crossed, where you want the whole pattern at a glance.
cards.commonMistake: Passing the long, unpivoted frame. heatmap can't reshape; it colours the table you hand it.

cards.prompt: Chart revenue against units to see whether they move together.
cards.why: Two numeric columns, one point per row — this is the plot that answers 'are these related?' before you reach for a correlation number.
cards.whenToUse: First look at the relationship between two measurements.
cards.commonMistake: Using lineplot for unordered data, which connects points that have no sequence and invents a trend.

cards.prompt: Same scatter, but colour each point by its category.
cards.why: hue= works the same way on every seaborn plot: name a column and it becomes colour, with a legend. One keyword turns a two-variable chart into a three-variable one.
cards.whenToUse: Checking whether a relationship holds inside every group or only overall.
cards.commonMistake: Using hue for a column with many distinct values, which produces a legend nobody can read. Past a handful of groups, facet instead.

cards.prompt: Scatter revenue against units and draw the best-fit line through it.
cards.why: regplot is scatterplot plus a fitted line and its confidence band — seaborn runs the regression for you, so you see the trend and how sure it is in one call.
cards.whenToUse: Showing a trend, not just the cloud of points.
cards.commonMistake: Treating the line as proof of a relationship. regplot will happily fit a line through noise; the confidence band is the part that tells you whether to believe it.

cards.prompt: Chart revenue over time with seaborn.
cards.why: Unlike pandas, seaborn takes the x column by name — no set_index() first. It sorts by x for you, so an out-of-order frame still draws a sensible timeline.
cards.whenToUse: A time series held in ordinary columns.
cards.commonMistake: Setting the index first out of pandas habit, then finding x='date' no longer resolves because date is no longer a column.

cards.prompt: Which call draws one small bar chart per region, side by side?
cards.answer: sns.catplot(data=df, x='category', y='revenue', col='region', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
cards.why: col= splits the data into one panel per value — small multiples. Every panel shares a scale, which is what makes them comparable; that is the whole point of faceting over one crowded chart.
cards.whenToUse: More groups than hue= can colour readably.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for catplot's axes-level cousins (barplot, boxplot). Only the figure-level functions — catplot, relplot, displot — can facet.
distractors: sns.catplot(data=df, x='category', y='revenue', row='region', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
sns.catplot(data=df, x='category', y='revenue', hue='region', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
sns.catplot(data=df, x='region', y='revenue', col='category', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)

cards.why: Three boxes means three categories on the x-axis, and region is the column with three values. The rule inside each box is the median, and the box itself spans the middle half of that region's revenue.
cards.whenToUse: Reading a distribution chart back to the code that made it.
cards.commonMistake: Counting the boxes without checking which column has that many values — the number of boxes tells you which column is on x.

cards.why: Regions run down the side and categories across the top, so region was the pivot's index and category its columns. Swap them in the pivot and the grid transposes.
cards.whenToUse: Working out which way round someone pivoted before plotting.
cards.commonMistake: Ignoring which labels sit on which axis. In a heatmap the pivot's index is always the rows.

cards.answer: sns.catplot(data=df, x='category', y='revenue', col='region', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
cards.why: One panel per region, each holding a bar per category — so region is the facet and category is the x-axis. The panels also share one y-scale, which is why North's bars look genuinely short rather than filling their panel.
cards.whenToUse: Telling a facet grid apart from a single chart with hue.
cards.commonMistake: Mixing up which column facets and which sits on x. Count the panels: that is the faceting column's value count.
distractors: sns.catplot(data=df, x='region', y='revenue', col='category', kind='bar', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
sns.barplot(data=df, x='category', y='revenue', hue='region', estimator='sum', errorbar=None)
